governanceNotes: D1 batch 60 (2026-09-26): one bounded association edge authored - memory-loss to depressive-disorder (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true. The proposition rests on the 14,961-participant three-wave cross-lagged panel network analysis (PMID 40550276) and the 2,365-participant ACTIVE longitudinal cohort (PMID 40939773), with the late-onset-depression cohort (PMID 41804263) carried on the edge as the documented reverse-direction counterweight.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-26: (i) reciprocity - the anchor cross-lagged study supports both vulnerability (memory to depression) and scar (depression to cognition) theories, with the reverse pathway more prominent in men and the forward pathway more prominent in women; (ii) prodromal overlap - subjective cognitive decline is framed in the located literature as an early symptomatic phase of Alzheimer disease, so the neurodegenerative attribution route is explicitly excluded from this edge; (iii) construct overlap - cognitive complaints are themselves symptoms of major depression, so shared-item contamination is recorded as a gap; (iv) direction guard - the insomnia and dementia propositions were withheld because the located material runs the opposite direction; (v) sibling-window discipline - cognitive-disorder, alzheimer-s-disease, and insomnia windows keep their own evidence and none is recycled (ME-29).

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Memory complaints document later depressive symptoms at large prospective-cohort level: the three-wave cross-lagged panel network analysis of 14,961 Chinese adults aged 45 and older found cognitive functions, particularly memory and orientation, predicted depressive symptoms at the earlier interval while hopelessness and low energy contributed to later cognitive decline, with memory a key bridge symptom and the cognitive-to-depressive pathway more prominent in women (PMID 40550276), and the ACTIVE longitudinal study of 2,365 older adults found subjective memory problems independently linked to more depressive symptoms alongside worse physical and social functioning (PMID 40939773); the relationship is recorded as documented reciprocal association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: both anchors are observational with the cross-lagged design explicitly supporting reciprocal vulnerability and scar pathways in opposite directions, so whether any individual depressive episode followed memory decline requires individual longitudinal clinical review with exclusion of the documented reverse direction.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Subjective and objective memory decline erodes daily function, self-efficacy, and social participation so hopelessness and low mood develop and depressive symptoms result, the functional-erosion route consistent with the cross-lagged memory-to-depression pathway and the ACTIVE cohort's parallel depressive-symptom signal, but whether this route produced any individual depression remains hypothesized until longitudinal symptom records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at observational cohort class only: the cross-lagged panel explicitly demonstrates bidirectional effects (depression-to-cognition was more prominent in men) and the authors state causal inference is limited by design; the ACTIVE cohort is a volunteer cognitive-training cohort with subjective memory measures; and both populations are community-dwelling and geographically bounded.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No randomized evidence establishes direction; the anchor study documents the reverse pathway (hopelessness and low energy predicting later cognitive decline) as prominently as the forward one; late-onset depression itself predicts cognitive impairment and dementia (PMID 41804263), complicating attribution; subjective memory complaints overlap with depression's cognitive symptoms; and neurodegenerative disease, sleep disturbance, medication effects, and social isolation are co-determinants.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: depression-related cognitive dysfunction (the documented reverse pathway; scar theory)
neurodegenerative prodrome including Alzheimer disease and subjective cognitive decline
sleep-disorder-related cognitive symptoms (the published insomnia window)
social isolation and sensory impairment in aging

evidenceGaps: No randomized evidence establishes direction; the anchor study documents the reverse pathway (hopelessness and low energy predicting later cognitive decline) as prominently as the forward one; late-onset depression itself predicts cognitive impairment and dementia (PMID 41804263), complicating attribution; subjective memory complaints overlap with depression's cognitive symptoms; and neurodegenerative disease, sleep disturbance, medication effects, and social isolation are co-determinants.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the prospective-memory-to-mood precedent with the reciprocal-pathway limit carried openly: the three-wave cross-lagged panel network analysis of 14,961 adults found memory and orientation predicted depressive symptoms at the earlier interval with memory as a key bridge symptom and the cognitive-to-depressive pathway more prominent in women (PMID 40550276), and the ACTIVE longitudinal cohort of 2,365 older adults found subjective memory problems independently linked to more depressive symptoms (PMID 40939773); because the same cross-lagged study documents the reverse pathway (hopelessness and low energy predicting later cognitive decline, more prominent in men) and late-onset depression independently predicts cognitive impairment and dementia (PMID 41804263), the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only, records the reciprocity openly, and routes individual claims through longitudinal clinical review with neurodegenerative, sleep, and medication exclusion.

sourceReferences.citation: Ma X, Zhou X, Qiu Y. Bidirectional relationships between cognitive decline and depression: A study of middle-aged and older adults using cross-lagged panel network analysis J Affect Disord. 2025 Nov 15;389:119741. doi: 10.1016/j.jad.2025.119741. PMID 40550276.
sourceReferences.note: Three-wave (2015/2018/2020) cross-lagged panel network analysis of CHARLS, 14,961 adults aged 45+: memory and orientation predicted depressive symptoms at the earlier interval; hopelessness and low energy contributed to later cognitive decline; memory and hopelessness were key bridge symptoms; cognitive-to-depressive pathways more prominent in females; supports the bounded reciprocal association only.
